In 1780 Kratzenstein won the prize of the Imperial Academy in St Petersburg and built the first free-reed instrument in the West; Vogler built the first free-reed organ on that idea. In 1810 Grenié exhibited an 'expressive organ', and in 1840 Debain took out a patent for the harmonium. From the middle of the nineteenth century the United States and Canada manufactured them in quantity; the American instrument changed to a suction bellows, adopted by Mason & Hamlin after 1885. Later the instrument reached India, Japan and China; under Japanese rule it was introduced into primary and secondary school music rooms in Taiwan, and by the end of the twentieth century it was gradually being displaced.

The harmonium, also called the pump organ, is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 412.132. It sounds with free reeds: the player treads the pedals to drive air through thin metal reeds in frames; the keyboard controls the pitch, the stops change the timbre, and the usual range is about three to five octaves. In Europe and North America it was common in small nineteenth-century churches, chapels and private houses; in the Indian subcontinent Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims use it for religious music such as qawwali, ghazal, kirtan and bhajan.
